questions.stem: Find the square roots of \(-3-4i\).

steps.explain: Let the square root be \(x+iy\) with \(x,y\) real, and expand \((x+iy)^{2}=x^{2}-y^{2}+2xyi\).
Equate real parts and imaginary parts.
Find \(y\) from \(xy=-2\): \(x=1\Rightarrow y=-2\); \(x=-1\Rightarrow y=2\) (the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) are OPPOSITE).
Check: \((1-2i)^{2}=1-4i+4i^{2}=1-4i-4=-3-4i\) ✓. Option B squares to \(-3+4i\); option C squares to \(3-4i\).
So the correct choice is option A.

Why not the others: the sign of the imaginary part must be negative; \(-\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{2}{3}i\) wrongly divides real by real and imaginary by imaginary.

questions.stem: If \(A=6-4i\) and \(B=-8+6i\), evaluate the following: \(\sqrt{B}\)
questions.hint: Let \(\sqrt{B}=x+iy\) with \(x,y\) real. Square it and equate the real and imaginary parts to \(-8\) and \(6\). A square root has TWO values (\(\pm\)).

steps.explain: Let \((x+iy)^{2}=-8+6i\) and expand the left side.
Equate real parts and imaginary parts.
From \(xy=3\): \(y=\dfrac{3}{x}\). Substitute into the first equation.
Factorise as a quadratic in \(x^{2}\): \((x^{2}-1)(x^{2}+9)=0\). Since \(x\) is real, \(x^{2}=1\) (not \(-9\)).
Find \(y\) from \(y=\dfrac{3}{x}\): \(x=1\Rightarrow y=3\); \(x=-1\Rightarrow y=-3\).

Both roots: \(\sqrt{B}=\pm(1+3i)\). Check: \((1+3i)^{2}=1+6i-9=-8+6i\) ✓. Why not the others: \(1+3i\) alone misses the root \(-(1+3i)\); \((3+i)^{2}=8+6i\) and \((1-3i)^{2}=-8-6i\) do not equal \(B\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Square (x + iy) and equate real and imaginary parts.

questions.stem: Consider the complex number \(z=a+ib\). The product of \(z\) and \(\overline{z}\) is 25. The sum of \(z\) and \(\overline{z}\) is 8. Find \(z\).
questions.hint: Use the two facts: \(z\overline{z}=|z|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\) and \(z+\overline{z}=2\,\mathrm{Re}(z)=2a\). Solve for \(a\) first, then \(b\). Remember \(b^{2}=9\) gives TWO values of \(b\).

steps.explain: \(z\overline{z}=(a+ib)(a-ib)=a^{2}+b^{2}\) (the \(i\) terms cancel), so \(a^{2}+b^{2}=25\).
\(z+\overline{z}=(a+ib)+(a-ib)=2a\), so \(2a=8\).
Substitute \(a=4\) into (1): \(16+b^{2}=25\Rightarrow b^{2}=9\Rightarrow b=\pm3\).
So \(z\) is either \(4+3i\) or \(4-3i\) (these are conjugates, and both satisfy the conditions).

Check \(z=4+3i\): \(z\overline{z}=16+9=25\) ✓; \(z+\overline{z}=8\) ✓. Why not the others: B has \(a=3\) (then the sum would be 6); C uses \(b^{2}=25\) (forgot to subtract \(a^{2}\)); D omits the conjugate solution \(4-3i\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(z\overline{z}=a^{2}+b^{2}\); \(z+\overline{z}=2a\).

\(i^{2}=-1\). Real parts: \(-\sqrt3-1\). Imaginary parts: \(-\sqrt3+1\).
Why not the others: B has the wrong real part (\(i^{2}\) should give \(-1\), not \(+1\)); C has the sign of \(\sqrt3\) wrong in the imaginary part; D is just \(w\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: If \(a=5+3i\) and \(b=3-4i\), evaluate \(\dfrac{a}{b}\).
questions.hint: To divide complex numbers, multiply top and bottom by the CONJUGATE of the denominator. Then the denominator becomes the real number \(x^{2}+y^{2}\).

steps.explain: The conjugate of \(b=3-4i\) is \(3+4i\). Multiply numerator and denominator by it (this multiplies by 1).
Denominator: \((3-4i)(3+4i)=3^{2}+4^{2}=25\) (difference of squares, \(i^{2}=-1\)).
Numerator: expand and use \(i^{2}=-1\).
Divide each part by 25.
Why not the others: B uses \(i^{2}=+1\) (giving 27); C has the wrong sign; D divides by 5 instead of 25 (the denominator is \(3^{2}+4^{2}=25\), not 5).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(3+4i\).

questions.stem: Consider two complex numbers, \(u\) and \(v\), such that \(\operatorname{Im}(u)=2\) and \(\operatorname{Re}(v)=1\). Given that \(u+v=-uv\), find the values of \(u\) and \(v\).
questions.hint: Write \(u=a+2i\) and \(v=1+bi\) with \(a,b\) REAL. Expand \(u+v\) and \(-uv\), equate real parts and imaginary parts, and solve the two equations. Always check that the answers are real.

steps.explain: Let \(u=a+2i\) and \(v=1+bi\) (\(a,b\in\mathbb R\)). Compute \(u+v\).
Compute \(uv\) then \(-uv\): \(uv=(a+2i)(1+bi)=a+abi+2i+2bi^{2}=(a-2b)+(ab+2)i\).
Equate REAL parts: \(a+1=2b-a\).
Equate IMAGINARY parts: \(b+2=-(ab+2)\).
Substitute \(a=\dfrac{2b-1}{2}\) into \(ab+b+4=0\): \(\dfrac{b(2b-1)}{2}+b+4=0\). Multiply by 2.
Discriminant: \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\) with \(a=2,b=1,c=8\): \(1-64=-63<0\). So there is NO real value of \(b\).
But \(b\) must be real (it is the imaginary part of \(v\)). Therefore no such \(u\) and \(v\) exist.
Why not the others: each of B, C, D fails the equation: e.g. B: \(u+v=3+i\) but \(-uv=-(2+2i)(1-i)=-4\); C and D similarly do not satisfy \(u+v=-uv\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(u=a+2i\), \(v=1+bi\); equate real/imag; discriminant \(<0\).

questions.stem: If the complex number \(z\) satisfies \(|z|-z-4(1-2i)=0\), which of the following is \(|z|^{2}\)?
questions.hint: \(|z|\) is a REAL number. Rearrange to get \(z=|z|-4+8i\) and let \(r=|z|\). Then use \(|z|^{2}=\) (real part)\(^{2}+\)(imaginary part)\(^{2}\) to get an equation in \(r\).

steps.explain: Let \(r=|z|\) (a real number). Rearrange: \(z=r-4(1-2i)=r-4+8i\).
The real part of \(z\) is \(r-4\) and the imaginary part is \(8\), so \(|z|^{2}=(r-4)^{2}+8^{2}\). But \(|z|=r\).
Expand \((r-4)^{2}=r^{2}-8r+16\) and cancel \(r^{2}\) from both sides.
Why not the others: 80 is \(8r\) (an intermediate value); 180 and 400 do not satisfy \(r^{2}=(r-4)^{2}+64\).
So the correct choice is option C.

steps.explain: Take the square root of both sides.
Let \(\sqrt{-4+3i}=a+bi\) and square.
Use the modulus: \(a^2+b^2=|-4+3i|=\sqrt{16+9}=5\).
Add and subtract the equations \(a^2-b^2=-4\) and \(a^2+b^2=5\).
Signs: \(2ab=3>0\) means \(a\) and \(b\) have the SAME sign.
Add to \(1+2i\).
steps.work: \(z=1+2i\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(1+3i)\), i.e. the two solutions in the first option → A

questions.stem: By letting \((x+iy)^{2}=3-4i\), find \(\sqrt{3-4i}\).
questions.hint: Expand \((x+iy)^{2}\), equate real and imaginary parts, then solve the simultaneous equations (\(x,y\) real).

steps.explain: Expand \((x+iy)^{2}=x^{2}-y^{2}+2xyi\) and equate with \(3-4i\).
Equate real parts and imaginary parts.
From (2), \(y=-\dfrac{2}{x}\). Substitute into (1) and clear the fraction.
Factorise: \(\left(x^{2}-4\right)\left(x^{2}+1\right)=0\). Since \(x\) is real, \(x^{2}+1\ne0\), so \(x^{2}=4\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Equate real and imaginary parts; x and y are real.

questions.stem: Hence solve the equation \(z^{2}+(4-i)z+(3-i)=0\).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic formula. The discriminant simplifies to \(3-4i\), whose square root you found in part (i).

steps.explain: Identify \(a=1\), \(b=4-i\), \(c=3-i\) and work out the discriminant \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\).
So \(\sqrt{\Delta}=\sqrt{3-4i}=\pm(2-i)\) from part (i).
Use the quadratic formula \(z=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\).
Check: sum of roots \(=-4+i=-(4-i)\) and product \(=(-1)(-3+i)=3-i\) \(\checkmark\). (The roots are not conjugates, because the coefficients are not real.)
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Quadratic formula; the discriminant equals the number from part (i).

questions.stem: Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation \(z^{2}-3z+(3+i)=0\).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic formula. The discriminant \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\) is \(-3-4i\), whose square roots you found in part (i).

steps.explain: Quadratic formula with \(a=1,\ b=-3,\ c=3+i\).
Discriminant: \(9-12-4i=-3-4i\).
From part (i), \(\sqrt{-3-4i}=\pm(1-2i)\).
Take the two signs separately.
Check with sum and product of roots: \((2-i)+(1+i)=3\) ✓ (equals \(-b\)) and \((2-i)(1+i)=2+2i-i-i^{2}=3+i\) ✓ (equals \(c\)). Option C forgets to divide by 2.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Quadratic formula, then use the square root from part (i).

questions.stem: Solve the following quadratic equation: \(ix^{2}-2(i+1)x+10=0\).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic formula with COMPLEX coefficients \(a=i\), \(b=-2(i+1)\), \(c=10\). You will need \(\sqrt{\Delta}\) of a complex number — find it by setting \((p+qi)^{2}=\Delta\). Then CHECK each answer in the original equation.

steps.explain: Identify the coefficients.
Discriminant \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\). First \(b^{2}=(-2-2i)^{2}=4(1+i)^{2}=4(1+2i-1)=8i\). Then \(4ac=4\times i\times10=40i\).
Quadratic formula: \(x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}=\dfrac{(2+2i)\pm(4-4i)}{2i}\).

Divide by \(2i\) by multiplying top and bottom by \(-i\) (since \(\dfrac{1}{i}=-i\)): \(\dfrac{6-2i}{2i}=\dfrac{(6-2i)(-i)}{2}=\dfrac{-6i+2i^{2}}{2}=-1-3i\), and \(\dfrac{-2+6i}{2i}=\dfrac{(-2+6i)(-i)}{2}=\dfrac{2i-6i^{2}}{2}=3+i\).

Check \(x=3+i\): \(x^{2}=8+6i\), so \(ix^{2}=8i-6\). Also \(-2(i+1)x=-2(i+1)(3+i)=-2(2+4i)=-4-8i\). Sum: \((-6+8i)+(-4-8i)+10=0\) ✓. Sum of the roots should be \(\dfrac{-b}{a}=\dfrac{2+2i}{i}=(2+2i)(-i)=2-2i\) and \((3+i)+(-1-3i)=2-2i\) ✓. Why not the others: the sums of their roots are \(-2i\), \(-11+i\) and \(-2i\), none equal to \(2-2i\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: \(a=i\); \(\Delta=-32i\); \(\sqrt{\Delta}=\pm(4-4i)\); sum of roots \(=2-2i\).

questions.stem: It is known that \(1+2i\) is one of the square roots of \(4i-3\). Using this fact, or otherwise, solve \(z^{2}-5z+7-i=0\).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic formula. The discriminant simplifies to \(4i-3\), whose square roots are \(\pm(1+2i)\) — you are given that! Remember BOTH roots: \(\pm\).

steps.explain: Quadratic formula with \(a=1\), \(b=-5\), \(c=7-i\).
Discriminant: \(25-28+4i=-3+4i=4i-3\).
Given \(1+2i\) is a square root of \(4i-3\): check \((1+2i)^{2}=1+4i+4i^{2}=-3+4i\) ✓. Square roots come in a pair \(\pm(1+2i)\).
Substitute and split into the two cases.
Simplify.
Check the sum of roots \(=(3+i)+(2-i)=5=-b\) ✓ and the product \((3+i)(2-i)=6-3i+2i-i^{2}=7-i=c\) ✓. Why not the others: B and C have wrong signs; D uses only one of the two square roots.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Quadratic formula; \(\sqrt{4i-3}=\pm(1+2i)\).

meta.source: Hills Grammar 2025 Trial HSC Mathematics Extension 2

questions.hint: Quadratic formula works for COMPLEX coefficients: \(z=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\) with \(b=-2i\). Remember \((-2i)^{2}=4i^{2}=-4\) and \(\sqrt{-12}=2i\sqrt3\).

steps.explain: \(z=\dfrac{2i\pm\sqrt{-12}}{2}=\dfrac{2i\pm2\sqrt3\,i}{2}\).
Factor out \(i\).

Check the sum of roots: \(i(1+\sqrt3)+i(1-\sqrt3)=2i\) ✓ (\(-\dfrac{b}{a}=2i\)). Why not the others: B has the real part 1 (the roots are NOT a conjugate pair because the coefficient \(-2i\) is not real); C uses \(\sqrt5\); D has the wrong overall sign.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Quadratic formula; \(\sqrt{-12}=2\sqrt3\,i\).

questions.stem: Hence, or otherwise, solve \(z^{2}-(1-i)z+6+2i=0\).
questions.hint: Quadratic formula with complex coefficients: \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\). If \(\Delta=-24-10i\), use the square roots from part (i): \(\sqrt\Delta=\pm(1-5i)\).

steps.explain: \(\sqrt\Delta=\pm(1-5i)\) from part (i). \(z=\dfrac{(1-i)\pm(1-5i)}{2}\).
The other root.

Check: sum of roots \(=1-3i+2i=1-i\) ✓ (\(-\dfrac{b}{a}\)); product \(=2i(1-3i)=2i+6=6+2i\) ✓. Why not the others: B are the conjugates (roots are NOT conjugates here because coefficients are not real); C, D are slips.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\Delta=-24-10i\); use part (i).

meta.source: Hunters Hill High School 2020 Trial Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Hence, solve \(z^{2}-(1-i)z+6+2i=0\).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic formula \(z=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\) with \(a=1\), \(b=-(1-i)\), \(c=6+2i\). The discriminant \(\Delta\) is the number whose square root you just found.

steps.explain: Discriminant \(\Delta=b^{2}-4ac\). First \((1-i)^{2}=1-2i+i^{2}=-2i\).
Great: it is exactly the number from part (i), so \(\sqrt\Delta=\pm(1-5i)\).
Quadratic formula: \(z=\dfrac{(1-i)\pm(1-5i)}{2}\).
Other root.
Check the sum of roots \(=1-i\): \((1-3i)+2i=1-i\) ✓. Check the product \(=6+2i\): \((1-3i)(2i)=2i-6i^{2}=6+2i\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the signs reversed; C and D do not have sum \(1-i\) and product \(6+2i\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\Delta=-24-10i\); use part (i).

questions.stem: If \(z=2-i\), which graph best represents \(w=-\overline{z}+2i\) ?
questions.hint: Find \(\overline{z}\) (conjugate), then negate it, then add \(2i\), and read off the point.

steps.explain: Conjugate of \(z=2-i\).
Negate.
Add \(2i\).
The point \((-2,1)\) is in the second quadrant (left and up).
This is graph A → A

keyPoints.note: Compute \(w=-2+i\) and locate it.

questions.hint: Do it in two moves: \(\bar{z}\) reflects \(z\) in the real axis; multiplying by \(i\) rotates by \(90^{\circ}\) anticlockwise. Or use \(z=x+iy\) and work out \(i\bar{z}\) algebraically.

steps.explain: Read \(z\) from the diagram: it is in the first quadrant, roughly \(z=x+iy\) with \(x\approx0.5\) and \(y\approx1\).

steps.explain: Multiply by \(i\): \(i\bar{z}=i(x-iy)=ix-i^{2}y=y+ix\).

So the real part is \(y\) and the imaginary part is \(x\): the point \((x,y)\) becomes \((y,x)\). With \(x\approx0.5\), \(y\approx1\): \(i\bar{z}\approx1+0.5i\), in the first quadrant, flatter than \(z\) (green).

steps.explain: Expand \(-i(a+bi)\), using \(i^{2}=-1\).
Read off the new point: real part \(=b\) (positive, small), imaginary part \(=-a\) (negative, large, since \(a>b\) in the diagram).
Geometrically: the point is rotated \(90^{\circ}\) clockwise (orange arrow). A first-quadrant point near the real axis moves into the fourth quadrant near the NEGATIVE imaginary axis.

questions.stem: Given that \(z=5e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}\), which expression is equal to \((\overline{z})^{-1}\) ?
questions.hint: Conjugate flips the argument; reciprocal flips it again and inverts the modulus.

steps.explain: Read off the modulus and argument of \(z\).
The conjugate keeps the modulus and changes the sign of the argument.
Taking the reciprocal (power \(-1\)) inverts the modulus and changes the sign of the argument again.
Write it in cos–sin form.
Both the conjugate and the reciprocal flip the argument, so the two sign changes cancel. Option C forgets that the reciprocal flips it back.

keyPoints.note: Two operations: conjugate (arg → −arg) then reciprocal (|z| → 1/|z|, arg → −arg).

questions.stem: Given that \(z = \sqrt2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \sqrt2 i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), express \(z\) in the form \(x+iy\), where \(x\) and \(y\) are real numbers, in exact form.
questions.hint: Use \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac12\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Multiply carefully by \(\sqrt2\).

steps.explain: Write the known exact values: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac12\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
Substitute into z. The real part is \(\sqrt2\times\dfrac12\) and the imaginary part is \(-\sqrt2\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
Simplify each part. \(\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) and \(\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\).
Check the signs: the real part is positive (cos is positive) and the imaginary part is negative because of the minus sign in front of i.

keyPoints.note: Keep surds exact; do not use decimals.

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: Evaluate \(z^{10}\), leaving your answer in modulus argument form (for the same \(z\) as in part (i)).
questions.hint: Write z in modulus-argument form first: modulus \(\sqrt2\), argument \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Then use de Moivre's theorem.

steps.explain: Find the modulus of z: \(|z| = \sqrt{\left(\sqrt2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^2}=\sqrt2\).
The argument is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (the z in the question is \(\sqrt2\cos\theta - i\sqrt2\sin\theta = \sqrt2\,\mathrm{cis}(-\theta)\)).
Apply de Moivre's theorem: \(z^{10} = (\sqrt2)^{10}\,\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\right)+i\sin\left(-\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\right)\right)\). Here \((\sqrt2)^{10}=2^5=32\).
Reduce the angle by adding \(4\pi\) (a full turn is \(2\pi\)): \(-\dfrac{10\pi}{3}+4\pi=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

keyPoints.note: Find |z| and arg z, then use de Moivre.

questions.stem: Let \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\). Express \(z\) in the form \(e^{i\theta}\), where \(\theta\) is the argument of \(z\).
questions.hint: Find the modulus and the argument of \(z\). Then write \(z=|z|e^{i\theta}\).

steps.explain: Modulus: \(|z|=\sqrt{\dfrac14+\dfrac34}=1\).
Argument: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\div\dfrac{1}{2}=\sqrt3\). Both parts are positive, so \(z\) is in the first quadrant and \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
Write \(z=1\cdot e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\).
Check: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac12\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), matching \(z\). Common mistake: \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (using the wrong angle).

questions.stem: Evaluate \(z^i\) in exact form.
questions.hint: Substitute \(z=e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\) and use \(e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\)... remember \(i\cdot i=-1\).

steps.explain: Use \(z=e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\) from part (i): \(z^i=\left(e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\right)^i\).
Apply the index law \((e^a)^b=e^{ab}\): \(z^i=e^{i\cdot\frac{\pi}{3}i}\).
Check: the result is real and positive, as expected for a real exponential. Common mistake: \(e^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\) (forgetting \(i^2=-1\)).

options: \(OA\perp OB\), so the angles are all right angles.
\(OC=2\) because \(OC\) is a diagonal of length 2.
\(OA=OB\) (radii of the unit circle), and \(BC=OA\) and \(AC=OB\), so all four sides are equal.
\(OACB\) has two pairs of equal angles at O and C.
questions.hint: A rhombus has four equal sides. Use the equal radii and the parallelogram sides from \(\vec{OC}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}\).

steps.explain: Points A and B lie on the unit circle, so \(OA = OB = 1\) (both are radii).
Since \(\vec{OC}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}\), the figure is a parallelogram: \(BC=OA\) and \(AC=OB\).
Four sides, all equal in length, make a rhombus.
steps.work: Answer: all four sides equal (radii of the unit circle).

questions.stem: Show that \(\arg(z+w)=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}\), where \(z=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1+i)\) and \(w=i\).
questions.answer: Use the rhombus property: the diagonal OC bisects the angle AOB. \(\arg z=\dfrac\pi4\) and \(\angle BOA=\dfrac\pi4\), so \(\arg(z+w)=\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}\).
questions.hint: Find the argument of z and the angle between OA and OB, then use the fact that the diagonal bisects the angle.

steps.explain: \(\arg z=\dfrac\pi4\) (since \(z=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}i\)) and \(\arg w=\dfrac\pi2\). So \(\angle AOB=\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac\pi4\).
In a rhombus the diagonal bisects the angle. So \(\arg(z+w)=\arg z+\dfrac12\angle AOB=\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac\pi8\).
Add: \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{8}=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}\). Shown.

questions.stem: Hence, show that \(\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{8}=\sqrt2+1\).
questions.hint: Write \(z+w\) in the form \(x+iy\), then use \(\tan(\arg(z+w))=\dfrac{y}{x}\).

steps.explain: Write \(z+w=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+1\right)i\).
Then \(\tan(\arg(z+w))=\dfrac{1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}}=\sqrt2+1\).
From part (ii), \(\arg(z+w)=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}\), so \(\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{8}=\sqrt2+1\). Shown.

questions.stem: Let \(z=1+\sqrt{3}i\). What is \(z\) in exponential form?
questions.hint: Exponential form is \(z=re^{i\theta}\) with \(r=|z|\) and \(\theta=\arg z\). Find the modulus first, then the argument from the quadrant and the ratio of the parts.

steps.explain: Modulus.
Argument: \(z\) is in quadrant 1, so \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{Im}}{\text{Re}}=\sqrt{3}\).
Write in exponential form.
Why not A? It has modulus 1, but \(|z|=2\).

questions.stem: Let \(z=1+i\) and \(w=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Express \(\dfrac{w}{z}\) in polar form. Show all working.
questions.hint: Put \(z\) in polar form first (\(r=\sqrt{2}\), \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)). For a QUOTIENT: DIVIDE the moduli and SUBTRACT the arguments.

steps.explain: Polar form of \(z=1+i\).
Polar form of \(w\) (already given).
Quotient rule: \(\left|\dfrac{w}{z}\right|=\dfrac{|w|}{|z|}\) and \(\arg\dfrac{w}{z}=\arg w-\arg z\).
Write in polar form.

keyPoints.note: Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

questions.stem: Evaluate \(2e^{\frac{5\pi i}{6}}\) in Cartesian form.
questions.hint: Euler's formula: \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\). \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=150^\circ\) is in the second quadrant.

steps.explain: Use Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) with \(\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
\(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=150^\circ\) lies in the second quadrant, so cosine is NEGATIVE and sine is POSITIVE. The reference angle is \(30^\circ\).
Substitute and multiply by 2.
Check the quadrant: real part negative, imaginary part positive is the second quadrant, matching \(150^\circ\). Option A (fourth quadrant), B (first) and C (third) are in the wrong quadrant.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Convert Euler form to a + bi: 5pi/6 is 150 degrees, second quadrant.

questions.stem: If \(z=1-i\sqrt{3}\), express \(z\) in modulus/argument form.
questions.hint: Find \(|z|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\), then the argument from \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}\) with the correct quadrant.

steps.explain: Find the modulus: \(z=1-\sqrt{3}\,i\) has real part 1 and imaginary part \(-\sqrt{3}\).
Find the reference angle from \(\tan\alpha=\left|\dfrac{\text{Im}}{\text{Re}}\right|\).
The point \((1,-\sqrt{3})\) is in the FOURTH quadrant (real part positive, imaginary part negative), so the argument is negative: \(\arg z=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
Write in modulus-argument form \(r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).
Check: \(2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right)=1-\sqrt{3}\,i\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Modulus first, then argument; check the quadrant.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the equation \(\left|e^{-i\theta}-1\right|=2\)?
questions.hint: Write \(e^{-i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\), find the modulus squared, and solve for \(\cos\theta\). Or test the four options.

steps.explain: Write \(e^{-i\theta}\) in cartesian form: \(e^{-i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\) (it is a point on the unit circle).
Modulus squared \(=(\text{real part})^{2}+(\text{imaginary part})^{2}\).
Use \(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1\).
The modulus is 2, so the modulus squared is 4.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the complex number \(z=5\sqrt{3}-5i\)?
questions.hint: Exponential form is \(re^{i\theta}\) with \(r=|z|\) and \(\theta=\arg z\). Find the modulus first, then the argument, and check which QUADRANT \(z\) is in.

questions.stem: Write down the moduli and argument of \(-\sqrt{3}+i\)
questions.hint: Modulus \(=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\). For the argument find the acute reference angle with \(\tan^{-1}\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right|\), then use the QUADRANT: \(-\sqrt3+i\) has a negative real part and positive imaginary part, so it is in the 2nd quadrant.

steps.explain: Read off \(x=-\sqrt3\) and \(y=1\).
Modulus: \(r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\).
Reference angle: \(\tan\alpha=\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right|=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\), so \(\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
The point is in the SECOND quadrant (left and up), so the argument is \(\pi-\alpha\) (measured anticlockwise from the positive \(\mathrm{Re}\) axis).

questions.stem: Write down the moduli and argument of \(4+4i\)
questions.hint: Here \(x=y=4\), so the point lies on the line \(y=x\) at \(45^{\circ}\). The modulus is the length of the diagonal of a \(4\times4\) square.

questions.stem: Hence express in modulus/argument form \(\dfrac{-\sqrt3+i}{4+4i}\).
questions.hint: For a quotient: DIVIDE the moduli and SUBTRACT the arguments, \(\dfrac{r_1\operatorname{cis}\theta_1}{r_2\operatorname{cis}\theta_2}=\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1-\theta_2)\). Use parts (i) and (ii).

steps.explain: From (i): \(-\sqrt3+i=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\). From (ii): \(4+4i=4\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Divide the moduli: \(\dfrac{2}{4\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\) (rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by \(\sqrt2\)).
Subtract the arguments (common denominator 12): \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=\dfrac{10\pi}{12}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{12}\).
Check the range: \(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}=105^{\circ}\) is in \((-\pi,\pi]\) ✓.
Why not the others: B ADDS the arguments (\(\dfrac{10\pi+3\pi}{12}=\dfrac{13\pi}{12}\)); C multiplies the moduli instead of dividing; D subtracts incorrectly (\(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Divide moduli, subtract arguments.

questions.hint: Square \(z=x+iy\) directly: \(z^{2}=(x^{2}-y^{2})+2xy\,i\), so \(a=x^{2}-y^{2}\) and \(b=2xy\). Use the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) and the condition \(x<y\) (both negative).

steps.explain: Expand \(z^{2}=(x+iy)^{2}=x^{2}+2xyi+i^{2}y^{2}\) and separate real and imaginary parts.
Third quadrant: \(x<0\) and \(y<0\). So \(xy>0\) (negative \(\times\) negative), hence \(b=2xy>0\).
The condition \(x<y\) with BOTH negative means \(x\) is further from zero than \(y\): \(|x|>|y|\). (e.g. \(x=-2<y=-1\).) Hence \(x^{2}>y^{2}\) and \(a=x^{2}-y^{2}>0\).

So \(z^{2}\) has \(a>0\) and \(b>0\): first quadrant. Geometrically \(\arg z\) is between \(-\pi\) and \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) (the part of quadrant 3 above the line \(y=x\) is closer to the negative real axis); doubling gives an angle between \(-2\pi\) and \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), which is the same as between \(0\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

questions.stem: For the complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\), it is known that \(\dfrac{z}{w}\) is purely real with a modulus of 2. If \(z=4e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\), find \(w\) in exponential form.
questions.hint: “Purely real with modulus 2” means \(\dfrac{z}{w}=+2\) OR \(-2\). Solve \(w=\pm\dfrac{1}{2} z\) and write \(-1=e^{i\pi}\) or \(e^{-i\pi}\) when converting a negative sign to an argument.

steps.explain: A purely real number with modulus 2 is \(2\) or \(-2\) (two real numbers have modulus 2).
Rearrange for \(w\): \(w=\pm\dfrac{z}{2}\).
The \(+\) case: \(w=2e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}\).
The \(-\) case: \(-1=e^{-\pi i}\) (rotate by \(\pi\); choose \(-\pi\) so the argument stays in \((-\pi,\pi]\)). So \(-2e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}=2e^{\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\pi\right)i}=2e^{-\frac{2\pi}{3}i}\).

questions.stem: The complex number \(w\) lies on the unit circle with \(\mathrm{Arg}(w)=\theta\). Show that \(\dfrac{1+w}{1-w}=i\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}\).
questions.hint: Write \(w=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) and use the HALF-ANGLE identities: \(1+\cos\theta=2\cos^{2}\dfrac\theta2\), \(1-\cos\theta=2\sin^{2}\dfrac\theta2\), \(\sin\theta=2\sin\dfrac\theta2\cos\dfrac\theta2\). Then multiply top and bottom by \(i\) or by a conjugate.

steps.explain: \(w\) is on the unit circle, so \(|w|=1\) and \(w=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\). Write the numerator and denominator.

Factor: top \(=2c(c+is)\); bottom \(=2s(s-ic)\).
Note \(s-ic=-i(c+is)\) (check: \(-i\cdot c-i\cdot is=-ic+s\) ✓). So \((c+is)\) cancels.
\(\dfrac{1}{-i}=i\) (multiply top and bottom by \(i\)).

Why not the others: B drops the \(i\) (the quotient is purely IMAGINARY: the vectors \(1+w\) and \(1-w\) are at right angles, as the diagram shows); C has the wrong sign; D has \(\tan\) instead of \(\cot\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(1+\cos\theta=2\cos^{2}\dfrac\theta2\); \(1-\cos\theta=2\sin^{2}\dfrac\theta2\).

steps.explain: Arguments: \(\arg(\alpha z^{2})-\arg\alpha=2\arg z\). So \(2\arg z\approx108^{\circ}-34^{\circ}=74^{\circ}\).
Moduli: \(|\alpha|=1\) (on the unit circle) and \(|\alpha z^{2}|\approx0.73\), so \(|z|^{2}\approx0.73\).
So \(z\) is at about \(37^{\circ}\) (just a little more anticlockwise than \(\alpha\)) and fairly CLOSE to the unit circle (modulus about 0.85).

questions.stem: Let \(w=-\sqrt3+i\) and \(z=1+i\). Find \(w\) and \(z\) in mod-arg form.
questions.hint: Modulus \(r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\). Argument: find the related acute angle from \(\tan^{-1}\left|\dfrac{b}{a}\right|\) and use the QUADRANT of \(a+ib\) (\(w\) has a NEGATIVE real part: 2nd quadrant).

steps.explain: \(w=-\sqrt3+i\): modulus \(\sqrt{3+1}=2\). Related angle \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac\pi6\); 2nd quadrant: \(\pi-\dfrac\pi6\).
\(z=1+i\): modulus \(\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2\). Argument \(\tan^{-1}1=\dfrac\pi4\) (1st quadrant).
Why not the others: B forgets the 2nd quadrant (\(\dfrac\pi6\) is the related angle); C, D swap or mis-calculate the moduli.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: 2nd quadrant: \(\pi-\dfrac\pi6\).

questions.stem: Let \(w=-\sqrt3+i=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(z=1+i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4\), so \(wz=\left(-\sqrt3-1\right)+\left(1-\sqrt3\right)i\). Hence, find the exact value of \(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\).
questions.hint: Find \(wz\) in mod-arg form by MULTIPLYING moduli and ADDING arguments, then compare REAL (or imaginary) parts with part (i). Reduce the angle to a related angle in \(\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]\).

steps.explain: Multiply moduli, add arguments: \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{10\pi+3\pi}{12}=\dfrac{13\pi}{12}\).
Equate real parts with part (i): \(2\sqrt2\cos\dfrac{13\pi}{12}=-\left(\sqrt3+1\right)\). Since \(\cos\dfrac{13\pi}{12}=-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}\):

Complementary angles: \(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}\). Rationalise: \(\dfrac{\sqrt3+1}{2\sqrt2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\).

Check: \(\dfrac{2.449+1.414}{4}=0.966=\sin75^{\circ}\) ✓. Why not the others: B is \(\sin\dfrac\pi{12}\) (\(15^{\circ}\)); C is not a sine of that size (\(>1\)); D is \(\sin\dfrac\pi{12}\) in another form.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Hence, find the exact value of \(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\).
keyPoints.note: \(wz=2\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{13\pi}{12}\); compare real parts.

questions.stem: Suppose that \(1-i=e^{a+ib}\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) and \(-\dfrac\pi2<b<\dfrac\pi2\). Find the exact values of \(a\) and \(b\).
questions.hint: \(e^{a+ib}=e^{a}\,e^{ib}=e^{a}\operatorname{cis}b\): the MODULUS is \(e^{a}\) and the ARGUMENT is \(b\). Write \(1-i\) in mod-arg form (it is in the 4th quadrant: negative argument) and compare. Solve \(e^{a}=\sqrt2\) using \(\ln\).

steps.explain: Mod-arg form of \(1-i\): modulus \(\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2\); argument \(-\dfrac\pi4\) (4th quadrant).
Compare with \(e^{a}\operatorname{cis}b\): \(e^{a}=\sqrt2\) and \(b=-\dfrac\pi4\) (inside \(-\dfrac\pi2<b<\dfrac\pi2\) ✓).
Why not the others: B forgets that \(\ln\sqrt2=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2\); C has the wrong sign for the argument; D leaves \(e^{a}\) unsolved.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the exact values of \(a\) and \(b\).
keyPoints.note: \(e^{a+ib}=e^a\operatorname{cis}b\); modulus \(=e^a\).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the complex number \(4\sqrt3-4i\)?
questions.hint: Write \(4\sqrt3-4i\) in the form \(re^{i\theta}\): find the modulus \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), then the argument from the quadrant (real part positive, imaginary part negative).

steps.explain: Read off the real and imaginary parts: \(x=4\sqrt3\) (positive) and \(y=-4\) (negative), so the point is in the 4th quadrant.
Modulus: \(r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\).
Argument: reference angle from \(\tan\alpha=\dfrac{4}{4\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\), so \(\alpha=\dfrac\pi6\). In the 4th quadrant the argument is NEGATIVE.
Combine: \(re^{i\theta}\).
Check: \(8\left(\cos\dfrac\pi6-i\sin\dfrac\pi6\right)=8\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{i}{2}\right)=4\sqrt3-4i\) ✓.
Why not the others: A has the wrong modulus (4, not 8); B and D use \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\), which is in the 2nd quadrant (real part negative).
So the correct choice is option C.

questions.stem: Let \(z=\sqrt3+i\). Express \(z\) in modulus-argument form.
questions.hint: Modulus \(r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\). Argument from \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}\) and the quadrant (both parts positive: 1st quadrant).

steps.explain: Real part \(\sqrt3\), imaginary part \(1\): both positive, so 1st quadrant.
Modulus.
Argument: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\), so \(\theta=\dfrac\pi6\) (1st quadrant).
Combine.
Why not the others: B uses \(\tan\theta=\sqrt3\) (x and y swapped); C has modulus 4 (forgot the square root); D has the wrong sign (the imaginary part is positive).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}\).

questions.stem: If \(z=\sqrt2-\sqrt6\,i\), express \(z\) in modulus-argument form.
questions.hint: Modulus \(r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\); argument from \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}\) AND the quadrant (here \(x>0\), \(y<0\): 4th quadrant, so the argument is negative).

steps.explain: Real part \(\sqrt2\), imaginary part \(-\sqrt6\): 4th quadrant.
Modulus: \(\left(\sqrt2\right)^{2}=2\) and \(\left(\sqrt6\right)^{2}=6\).
Argument: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{-\sqrt6}{\sqrt2}=-\sqrt3\). The reference angle is \(\dfrac\pi3\) and the point is in the 4th quadrant, so \(\theta=-\dfrac\pi3\).
Combine.
Check: \(2\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\sqrt2\) ✓ and \(2\sqrt2\cdot\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-\sqrt6\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign (the imaginary part is negative); C has modulus \(8\) (forgot the square root); D uses \(\tan\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\) (x and y swapped).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); 4th quadrant \(\Rightarrow\) negative argument.

questions.stem: Let \(z\) be a complex number such that \(z^{2}=i\bar z\). Which of the following is a possible value for \(z\)?
questions.hint: Write \(z=re^{i\theta}\), so \(\bar z=re^{-i\theta}\) and \(i=e^{\frac{i\pi}{2}}\). Equate the MODULI and then the ARGUMENTS (an argument is only defined up to adding \(2\pi k\)).

steps.explain: Write everything in exponential form: \(z=re^{i\theta}\), \(\bar z=re^{-i\theta}\), \(i=e^{\frac{i\pi}{2}}\).
Compare MODULI: \(r^{2}=r\). Since \(z\ne0\) (the options are non-zero), \(r=1\).
Compare ARGUMENTS: they may differ by a multiple of \(2\pi\).
Solve for \(\theta\): \(\theta=\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac{2\pi k}{3}\). Take \(k=0\), \(1\), \(-1\).

Only \(\theta=\dfrac\pi6\) appears among the options. Check: \(z=e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}\) gives \(z^{2}=e^{\frac{i\pi}{3}}\) (angle \(60^{\circ}\)); \(\bar z\) has angle \(-30^{\circ}\) and multiplying by \(i\) rotates it by \(+90^{\circ}\) to \(60^{\circ}\) ✓.

Why not the others: \(\theta=-\dfrac\pi3\): \(3\theta=-\pi\ne\dfrac\pi2+2\pi k\); \(\theta=\dfrac\pi3\): \(3\theta=\pi\) (no); \(\theta=-\dfrac\pi6\): \(3\theta=-\dfrac\pi2\), which differs from \(\dfrac\pi2\) by \(\pi\), not by \(2\pi k\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: \(z=re^{i\theta}\): \(r=1\), \(3\theta=\dfrac\pi2+2\pi k\).

parts.answer: ABCD is a parallelogram, so AD ∥ BC and co-interior angles give \(\angle DCB=\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{3}\). Also \(|d-c|=|b-c|\), i.e. CD = CB. So \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) is \(\overrightarrow{CB}\) rotated anticlockwise by \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) with the same length: \(d-c=(b-c)\operatorname{cis}\frac{\pi}{3}=(b-c)\left(\frac12+\frac{i\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).

keyPoints.note: ∠DCB = π − 2π/3 = π/3 and CD = CB, so CD is CB rotated anticlockwise by π/3.

parts.hint: arg((a − d)/(b − d)) is the angle from DB to DA. The figure is a rhombus.

steps.explain: \(\arg\left(\frac{a-d}{b-d}\right)=\arg(a-d)-\arg(b-d)\): the angle turned anticlockwise from \(\overrightarrow{DB}\) to \(\overrightarrow{DA}\), i.e. \(\angle BDA\).
A parallelogram with a pair of equal adjacent sides (\(CD=CB\)) is a rhombus, and the diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles. So \(DB\) bisects \(\angle ADC=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

questions.hint: Reflect e^(iθ) in the real axis to get e^(−iθ), then rotate 90° anticlockwise for the factor i.

steps.explain: From the diagram, \(e^{i\theta}\) is in the second quadrant, a little past the imaginary axis: \(\frac\pi2\lt\theta\lt\pi\). All the options have modulus 1, so only the argument matters.
\(e^{-i\theta}\) has argument \(-\theta\): it is the reflection of \(e^{i\theta}\) in the real axis, so it lands in the third quadrant.
Multiplying by \(i\) rotates a point \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise (adds \(\frac\pi2\) to the argument).

Since \(\frac\pi2\lt\theta\lt\pi\), the new argument is between \(-\frac\pi2\) and 0: the fourth quadrant, close to the positive real axis (because \(\theta\) is only a little more than \(\frac\pi2\)).

Add to \(M\).

questions.stem: By finding \(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OB}}{\overrightarrow{OA}}\), show that \(\tan\angle AOB=\dfrac{1}{3}\). (Here \(\overrightarrow{OA}=2+i\), \(\overrightarrow{OB}=3+3i\).) What is \(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OB}}{\overrightarrow{OA}}\) in the form \(a+bi\)?
questions.hint: Divide complex numbers by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator \(2-i\).

steps.explain: Write the quotient and multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, \(2-i\).
Expand the numerator: \((3+3i)(2-i)=6-3i+6i-3i^{2}=6+3i+3=9+3i\).
Expand the denominator: \((2+i)(2-i)=4-i^{2}=5\).
Divide each part by 5.
The argument of \(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OB}}{\overrightarrow{OA}}\) is the angle from \(OA\) to \(OB\), that is \(\angle AOB\). \(\tan\) of the argument is imaginary part over real part.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Multiply by the conjugate; arg of the quotient is the angle between the vectors.

questions.stem: Hence show that \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Which statement gives the correct reason? (Use the diagram: \(\overrightarrow{OA}=2+i\), \(\overrightarrow{OB}=3+3i\).)
options: \(\tan\angle AOx=\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\tan\angle AOB=\dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(\angle BOx=\angle AOB-\angle AOx=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\tan\angle AOx=\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\tan\angle AOB=\dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(\angle AOx+\angle AOB=\angle BOx=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) because \(B=3+3i\) has \(\tan\angle BOx=1\)
\(\angle AOx=\angle AOB\) so each angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\)
questions.hint: Add the two angles at \(O\): \(\angle AOx\) and \(\angle AOB\) together make \(\angle BOx\). Find each angle's tangent.

steps.explain: Find \(\angle AOx\), the angle from the real axis to \(OA\). \(A=2+i\) so \(\tan\angle AOx=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

The angle from the real axis to \(OB\) is the sum of the two angles: \(\angle AOx+\angle AOB=\angle BOx\).
\(B=3+3i\) lies on the line \(y=x\), so \(\tan\angle BOx=\dfrac{3}{3}=1\) and \(\angle BOx=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Substitute the angles.
So the correct choice is option B.

questions.stem: Complex numbers \(z_{1}\), \(z_{2}\) and \(z_{3}\) are given on the Argand diagram (with \(z_{3}\) anticlockwise from \(z_{2}\) as seen from \(z_{1}\)). Consider the complex number \(z_{3}\) such that \(\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)+\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)^{2}=0\). Find \(\dfrac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}\) and express your answer in the form \(r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\).

questions.hint: Let \(w=\dfrac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}\). Divide the given equation by \(\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)^{2}\) to get a quadratic in \(w\). Then use the DIAGRAM to decide which of the two roots applies.

steps.explain: Divide every term of the equation by \(\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)^{2}\) (non-zero, since \(z_{2}\ne z_{1}\)).
Quadratic formula with \(a=1,b=-1,c=1\): discriminant \(1-4=-3\).
Convert to polar form: modulus \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{3}{4}}=1\); argument \(\pm\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\pm\dfrac\pi3\).

Which sign? Dividing by \(z_{2}-z_{1}\) rotates the direction of \(z_{2}-z_{1}\) onto the direction of \(z_{3}-z_{1}\). In the diagram \(z_{3}\) is ANTICLOCKWISE from \(z_{2}\) (as seen from \(z_{1}\)), so the angle is POSITIVE: \(+\dfrac\pi3\).

Consider the complex number \(z_{3}\) such that \(\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)+\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)^{2}=0\). Given that \(\dfrac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}=\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\), show that \(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}\) are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Which argument is correct?

options: The modulus is 1, so \(|z_{3}-z_{1}|=|z_{2}-z_{1}|\) (two sides equal). The argument is \(\dfrac\pi3\), so the angle at \(z_{1}\) is \(60^{\circ}\). An isosceles triangle with a \(60^{\circ}\) apex angle has two base angles of \(\dfrac{180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}}{2}=60^{\circ}\), so all three angles are \(60^{\circ}\): the triangle is equilateral.
The modulus is 1, so \(|z_{3}-z_{1}|=|z_{2}-z_{1}|\). Hence the triangle is equilateral.
The argument is \(\dfrac\pi3\), so the angle at \(z_{1}\) is \(60^{\circ}\). Hence the triangle is equilateral.
The argument is \(\dfrac\pi3\), so \(z_{3}-z_{1}=\dfrac\pi3\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)\). Hence the triangle is equilateral.
questions.hint: For a quotient: \(\left|\dfrac{a}{b}\right|=\dfrac{|a|}{|b|}\) gives a LENGTH RATIO and \(\arg\dfrac{a}{b}=\arg a-\arg b\) gives the ANGLE between the two sides. You need BOTH facts (equal sides AND a \(60^{\circ}\) angle).

steps.explain: Take the modulus of both sides. \(\left|\dfrac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}\right|=\left|\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right|=1\), so the two sides from \(z_{1}\) have EQUAL length.
Take the argument: \(\arg\dfrac{z_{3}-z_{1}}{z_{2}-z_{1}}=\arg(z_{3}-z_{1})-\arg(z_{2}-z_{1})=\dfrac\pi3\), which is the ANGLE between the two sides at \(z_{1}\).
An isosceles triangle with apex angle \(60^{\circ}\) has base angles \(\dfrac{180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}}{2}=60^{\circ}\). All three angles are \(60^{\circ}\) (so all three sides are equal).

questions.stem: Complex numbers \(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}\) are the vertices of an equilateral triangle, with \(\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(z_{3}-z_{1}\right)\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)+\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)^{2}=0\). Show that \(\dfrac{1}{z_{2}-z_{1}}+\dfrac{1}{z_{1}-z_{3}}+\dfrac{1}{z_{3}-z_{2}}=0\). Which working is correct?
options: Let \(a=z_{2}-z_{1}\) and \(b=z_{3}-z_{1}\). Then \(z_{1}-z_{3}=-b\) and \(z_{3}-z_{2}=b-a\). The sum is \(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{b}+\dfrac{1}{b-a}=\dfrac{b(b-a)-a(b-a)+ab}{ab(b-a)}=\dfrac{a^{2}-ab+b^{2}}{ab(b-a)}=0\), since \(a^{2}-ab+b^{2}=0\) is the given condition.
Since \(\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)+\left(z_{1}-z_{3}\right)+\left(z_{3}-z_{2}\right)=0\), the reciprocals of the three numbers also add up to 0.
Let \(a=z_{2}-z_{1}\) and \(b=z_{3}-z_{1}\). The sum is \(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{b}+\dfrac1{b-a}=\dfrac{a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}}{ab(b-a)}=0\) because \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\).
questions.hint: Set \(a=z_{2}-z_{1}\), \(b=z_{3}-z_{1}\); then write the other difference \(z_{3}-z_{2}=b-a\). Combine the three fractions over a common denominator and compare the numerator with the given equation \(b^{2}-ab+a^{2}=0\).

steps.explain: Common denominator \(ab(b-a)\). Numerators: \(\dfrac{1}{a}\to b(b-a)\); \(-\dfrac{1}{b}\to-a(b-a)\); \(\dfrac1{b-a}\to ab\).
Expand the numerator: \(b^{2}-ab-ab+a^{2}+ab\).
The numerator is exactly the left side of the given condition, which equals 0.

Why not the others: B has \(+ab\) in the numerator (the middle term is \(-2ab+ab=-ab\)); C is false reasoning (the sum of numbers being 0 says nothing about their reciprocals); D has \(-2ab\) (an arithmetic slip) and \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\) is not equal to 0 in general.
So the correct choice is option A.

topics.title: Curves and Regions in the Argand Diagram

questions.stem: Which locus represents \(\arg(z-i)=\arg(z+1)\)?
questions.hint: Equal arguments require parallel vectors in the same direction. First find their common line, then check which parts point the same way.
questions.solution: The two exterior rays on \(y=x+1\): \(x<-1\) or \(x>0\), excluding \(z=-1\) and \(z=i\).

steps.explain: Represent z by coordinates and form the two vectors from the fixed points −1 and i.

questions.stem: The Argand diagram representing \(\arg(z+i-1)+\frac{\pi}{4}=0\) is:
questions.hint: Rewrite as arg(z − (1 − i)) = −π/4: a ray from 1 − i at angle −π/4.

steps.explain: Write the expression inside the argument as \(z\) minus a fixed point.

\(\arg(z-z_1)=\alpha\) is a ray that starts at \(z_1\) (not included, since \(\arg 0\) is undefined) and makes angle \(\alpha\) with the positive real direction. Here \(z_1=1-i\), i.e. the point \((1,-1)\), and \(\alpha=-\frac\pi4\).
steps.work: \(\text{start }(1,-1)\ (\text{open circle}),\qquad\text{direction angle }-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\ (\text{down and to the right})\)

questions.stem:
Sketch the region in the complex plane where the inequalities \(1\le|z-i|\le2\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\ge0\) hold simultaneously.

Clearly mark in all \(x\) and \(y\) intercepts.
questions.hint: |z − i| is the distance from (0, 1); draw circles of radius 1 and 2 about that point, then keep y ≥ 0.

steps.explain: \(|z-i|\) is the distance from \(z\) to the point \(i=(0,1)\). So \(1\le|z-i|\le2\) is a closed annulus (ring) centred at \((0,1)\) between the circles of radius 1 and 2.

questions.answer: The region is the part of the annulus centred at \(i=(0,1)\) with radii 1 and 2 (both circles included) that lies on or above the real axis. The outer circle meets the real axis at \(x=\pm\sqrt3\); the inner circle touches it at the origin. On the imaginary axis the boundary points are \(y=0\), \(y=2\) and \(y=3\) (the point \(y=-1\) is excluded because \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\ge0\)). The segment \(-\sqrt3\le x\le\sqrt3\) of the real axis is part of the boundary.

keyPoints.note: This is a ring centred at (0, 1) with radii 1 and 2; then keep only the part with y ≥ 0.

questions.stem:
In an Argand diagram \(z\) is a point on the circle \(|z|=2\).

Given that \(\arg z=\theta\) and \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac{\pi}{2}\).

meta.source: Abbotsleigh 2021 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.stem: Draw a diagram to represent this information.
parts.hint: |z| = 2 is a circle of radius 2 about O; 0 < θ < π/2 is the first quadrant.

steps.explain: \(|z|=2\) means \(z\) is 2 units from the origin, so \(z\) lies on the circle centred at \(O\) with radius 2. It crosses the axes at \(\pm2\) and \(\pm2i\).
\(0 \lt \arg z \lt \frac\pi2\) puts \(z\) in the first quadrant. Draw \(Oz\) and mark \(\theta\) between the positive real axis and \(Oz\).

parts.answer: A circle centred at the origin with radius 2 (crossing the axes at \(\pm2\) and \(\pm2i\)), with the point \(z\) on the arc in the first quadrant, joined to \(O\), and the angle \(\theta\) marked between the positive real axis and \(Oz\).

keyPoints.note: Draw the circle of radius 2 about O and put z in the first quadrant with angle θ from the positive real axis.

parts.stem: Find, in terms of \(\theta\), an expression for \(\arg z^2\).
parts.hint: arg(z²) = 2 arg z.

steps.explain: Write \(z\) in modulus-argument form.
By de Moivre's theorem the modulus is squared and the argument is doubled.
Since \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac\pi2\), we have \(0 \lt 2\theta \lt \pi\), which is already a principal argument.

meta.source: Abbotsleigh 2021 4U Trials & Solutions

keyPoints.note: Multiplying complex numbers adds arguments, so arg(z²) = 2 arg z.

parts.stem:
Find, in terms of \(\theta\), giving brief reasons, an expression for:

(A) \(\arg(z+2)\)
parts.hint: z + 2 is the diagonal of a rhombus with sides z and 2.

steps.explain: Add \(z\) and \(2\) as vectors: they are adjacent sides of a parallelogram with vertices \(O\), \(2\), \(z+2\), \(z\).
In a rhombus the diagonal bisects the angle between the sides. The sides from \(O\) make angles \(0\) and \(\theta\) with the real axis.

Sketch the region in the complex plane showing the inequalities

\(1\le|z-1+i|\le2\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\le\arg(z-1+i)\le\pi\)
questions.hint: Both conditions are measured from the point 1 − i.

steps.explain: Rewrite with the centre visible: \(z-1+i=z-(1-i)\). So both conditions are measured from the point \(1-i\), i.e. \((1,-1)\).
\(1\le|z-(1-i)|\le2\): the ring between circles of radius 1 and 2 centred at \((1,-1)\), boundaries included (solid).
\(\frac{3\pi}{4}\le\arg\le\pi\): from \((1,-1)\), the region between the ray pointing up-left at \(135^\circ\) and the ray pointing straight left at \(180^\circ\).
Shade the part of the ring inside that sector (centre point excluded).

questions.stem: Let \(z\) and \(w\) be complex numbers where \(w=\dfrac{z-2}{z-i}\) and \(w\neq0\) is purely imaginary. Which describes the locus of \(z\)?
options: A circle with centre \(\left(1,\dfrac12\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{5}{2}\), excluding \(z=2\) and \(z=i\)
A circle with centre \(\left(1,\dfrac12\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\), excluding the points \(z=2\) and \(z=i\)
A circle with centre \((2,0)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\), excluding \(z=2\) and \(z=i\)
A circle with centre \(\left(1,-\dfrac12\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\), with no points excluded
questions.hint: Write \(z=x+iy\), rationalise the denominator, and set the real part of \(w\) to zero.

steps.explain: Let \(z=x+iy\). Then \(w=\dfrac{(x-2)+iy}{x+i(y-1)}\). Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(x-i(y-1)\).
Real part of \(w\) is \(\dfrac{x(x-2)+y(y-1)}{x^2+(y-1)^2}\). Since \(w\) is purely imaginary, this must be 0, so \(x(x-2)+y(y-1)=0\).
Complete the square: \((x-1)^2+\left(y-\dfrac12\right)^2=1+\dfrac14=\dfrac54\). So the centre is \(\left(1,\dfrac12\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\).
Exclude points where \(w\) is undefined or zero: \(w=0\) when \(z=2\), and \(z=i\) makes the denominator zero. Both lie on the circle, so they are excluded.
steps.work: Circle with centre \(\left(1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\), excluding \(z=2\) and \(z=i\).

questions.stem: The locus of \(z\) is displayed on the Argand diagram below (the straight line segment from \(i\) to \(1\), with both end points excluded). Which of the following is the equation of the locus of \(z\)?
questions.hint: \(\arg\left(\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=\arg(z-z_1)-\arg(z-z_2)\) is the angle at \(z\) subtended by the end points. Which angle does a point BETWEEN the two end points of a segment see?

steps.explain: The end points are \(z_1=i\) (the point \((0,1)\)) and \(z_2=1\) (the point \((1,0)\)). So the correct options are the ones with \(z-i\) and \(z-1\) (A or B).
For a point \(z\) ON the segment between them, the vectors \(z-i\) and \(z-1\) point in OPPOSITE directions (one towards each end point).
So \(\dfrac{z-i}{z-1}=-k\) is a NEGATIVE real number, whose argument is \(\pm\pi\) (not 0).
Why not A? \(\arg=0\) is the locus of points on the line OUTSIDE the segment (on the same side of both end points).

keyPoints.note: On the segment the two vectors point opposite ways, so the argument is plus or minus pi.

questions.stem: Sketch the intersection of the regions defined by \(|z-2i|\le1\) and \(0<\text{Arg}(z-2i)\le\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).
questions.answer: A sector of the disc with centre \(2i\) (the point \((0,2)\)) and radius 1: the part between the ray at angle \(0\) (the horizontal line to the right, drawn dashed, EXCLUDED) and the ray at angle \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) (solid, INCLUDED); the centre is excluded since the argument is undefined there.
questions.hint: Both conditions are measured from the CENTRE \(2i\): the first is a DISC; the second is a WEDGE (all points at angles between 0 and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) from the centre).

steps.explain: Region 1: \(|z-2i|\le1\) is every point at distance at most 1 from \(2i\): a solid disc, centre \((0,2)\), radius 1 (boundary included).

Region 2: \(\text{Arg}(z-2i)\) is the angle of the vector from \(2i\) to \(z\), measured from the positive real direction. \(0<\text{Arg}\le\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) is the wedge above the horizontal line through \(2i\), up to the ray at \(135^\circ\).
Boundaries: the ray at \(\theta=0\) is NOT included (dashed), the ray at \(\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) IS included (solid), and the centre \(2i\) is excluded (open circle).
The intersection of the two regions is the shaded sector of the disc.

questions.stem: Sketch the graph of the complex number \(z\) defined by \(\arg\left(\dfrac{z-2}{z+2i}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
questions.answer: The angle between the vectors from \(-2i\) to \(z\) and from \(2\) to \(z\) is a right angle, so \(z\) lies on the circle with diameter joining \(2\) and \(-2i\) (centre \(1-i\), radius \(\sqrt{2}\)). Test \(z=0\): \(\dfrac{0-2}{0+2i}=i\), which has argument \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) ✓, so the locus is the semicircle containing the origin (the upper-left semicircle), excluding its endpoints \(2\) and \(-2i\).
questions.hint: \(\arg\dfrac{z-2}{z+2i}=\arg(z-2)-\arg(z+2i)\) is the angle at \(z\) between the points \(-2i\) and \(2\). A right angle in a semicircle…

steps.explain: The argument of the quotient is the angle at \(z\) between the rays to \(-2i\) and \(2\): it equals \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
An angle of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in a semicircle: \(z\) lies on the circle with diameter \(-2i\) to \(2\) (centre \(1-i\), radius \(\sqrt{2}\)).
Which semicircle? Test \(z=0\): \(\dfrac{-2}{2i}=i\) has argument \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) ✓, so the origin is on the locus: the semicircle on the origin's side of the chord.
Sketch: the arc (not the full circle) from \(-2i\) to \(2\) through \(0\), with open circles at the endpoints.

keyPoints.note: A right angle at z means z is on a semicircle with the two points as diameter.

questions.hint: \(z-1+2i=z-(1-2i)\): the ray starts at the point \(1-2i\). A negative argument means the ray points below the horizontal.

steps.explain: Rewrite the expression so it has the form \(\operatorname{Arg}(z-z_{0})\): \(z-1+2i=z-(1-2i)\). So the ray starts at the point \(z_{0}=1-2i\), which is 1 to the right and 2 down from the origin.

steps.explain: \(\operatorname{Arg}(z-z_{0})=\theta\) is a ray from \(z_{0}\) at angle \(\theta\) measured from the positive real direction. \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=-60^\circ\) means turn \(60^\circ\) CLOCKWISE from the horizontal, so the ray points down and to the right.

Eliminate the others: B and D point up-right (positive argument \(+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\)). C and D start at \(-1+2i\), which would be \(\operatorname{Arg}(z+1-2i)\). Only diagram A starts at \(1-2i\) and points down-right.

questions.stem: The complex number \(z\) is represented by the point \(P\). Given that \(P\) moves in a way such that \(\dfrac{z-2}{z-i}\) is purely imaginary, sketch the locus of \(P\), show any intercepts and any key features. Which sketch is correct? (An open circle means the point is excluded.)

questions.hint: Put \(z=x+iy\), multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, and set the REAL part to zero. Then complete the square to get a circle, and exclude the points where the fraction is not purely imaginary (\(z=2\) gives 0, and \(z=i\) is undefined).

steps.explain: Let \(z=x+iy\) and multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, \(x-i(y-1)\).
Real part of the numerator: \((x-2)x+y(y-1)\). The denominator \(x^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\) is real, so the fraction is purely imaginary when the real part is 0.
Complete the square for \(x\) and \(y\): add \(1\) and \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) to both sides.

A circle with centre \(\left(1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx1.12\). Intercepts: \(y=0\Rightarrow(x-1)^{2}=1\Rightarrow x=0,2\); \(x=0\Rightarrow\left(y-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow y=0,1\). So it passes through \(O\), \(2\) and \(i\).

questions.stem: The equation, in Cartesian form, of the locus of the point \(z\) if \(|z+2i|=|z+4|\) is:
questions.hint: Write \(z=x+iy\) and group the real and imaginary parts inside each modulus. Then SQUARE both sides to remove the square roots and simplify.

steps.explain: Let \(z=x+iy\). Group real and imaginary parts: \(z+2i=x+(y+2)i\) and \(z+4=(x+4)+yi\).
Both moduli are equal, so their squares are equal.
Expand the brackets.
Cancel \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) from both sides.
Collect everything on one side, then divide by 4.

Meaning: \(|z+2i|\) is the distance from \(z\) to \(-2i\), and \(|z+4|\) is the distance from \(z\) to \(-4\). Points equidistant from the two fixed points \(-2i\) and \(-4\) lie on the PERPENDICULAR BISECTOR of the segment joining them (green line, through the midpoint \((-2,-1)\)). Check: \(2(-2)-(-1)+3=0\) ✓.

questions.stem: For a complex number \(z\), \(|z-1|=2|z+1|\). Find the Cartesian equation of the locus of \(z\).
questions.hint: Let \(z=x+iy\). Write each modulus squared, remembering that \(2|z+1|\) squared is \(4|z+1|^{2}\) (the 2 must be squared too).

steps.explain: Let \(z=x+iy\). Square both sides of \(|z-1|=2|z+1|\) (the 2 becomes 4).
Write each modulus squared in terms of \(x\) and \(y\): \(|a+bi|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\).
Expand both sides.
Bring everything to the right side.
The Cartesian equation of the locus is \(3x^{2}+10x+3y^{2}+3=0\).
Why not the others: B swaps \(z-1\) and \(z+1\) (sign of \(10x\)); C does not square the factor 2 (uses 2 instead of 4); D has a wrong constant sign.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the Cartesian equation of the locus of \(z\)
keyPoints.note: Square both sides; the factor 2 becomes 4.

questions.stem: For a complex number \(z\), \(|z-1|=2|z+1|\). Describe the locus of \(z\).
options: A circle with centre \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{3},0\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{4}{3}\)
A circle with centre \(\left(\dfrac{5}{3},0\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{4}{3}\)
A circle with centre \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{3},0\right)\) and radius \(\dfrac{16}{9}\)
questions.hint: Divide the equation \(3x^{2}+10x+3y^{2}+3=0\) by 3 so \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) have coefficient 1, then COMPLETE THE SQUARE in \(x\). Compare with \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\).

steps.explain: Divide by 3 so that the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are both 1 (equal coefficients mean a circle).
Complete the square: add \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\div2\right)^{2}=\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{25}{9}\) to both sides.
Factorise the \(x\)-terms and simplify the right side.
Compare with \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\): centre \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{3},0\right)\), and \(r^{2}=\dfrac{16}{9}\), so \(r=\dfrac{4}{3}\) (the square ROOT of \(\dfrac{16}{9}\)).

questions.hint: Do the two conditions one at a time. \(|z|\) is the DISTANCE from the origin (a ring between two circles). \(\arg z\) is the ANGLE from the positive real axis (a wedge). The region is where they overlap. Use a dashed line for \(<\) and a solid line for \(\le\).

steps.explain: Modulus condition \(1<|z|\le3\): points between the circle of radius 1 (NOT included, dashed) and the circle of radius 3 (included, solid): a ring.

Argument condition \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\arg z\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): the wedge from \(-60^{\circ}\) (below the real axis) to \(+45^{\circ}\) (above), measured from the positive real axis. Both rays are included (solid).
The region is the part of the ring inside the wedge: the green region (a piece of the ring on the RIGHT, containing the positive real axis).

questions.hint: \(|z|\) is the distance of \(z\) from the origin. \(1\le|z|\le2\) means the distance is BETWEEN 1 and 2 (a ring between two circles centred at \(0\)). “\(\ge\)” and “\(\le\)” include the boundary, so the circles are SOLID.

steps.explain: \(|z|=r\) is a circle with centre \(0\) and radius \(r\). So \(|z|=1\) and \(|z|=2\) are two concentric circles.
Rewrite \(2\ge|z|\ge1\) the usual way round: distance from the origin at least 1 and at most 2.
Points with \(|z|<1\) are inside the small circle and points with \(|z|>2\) are outside the big circle — neither is allowed. Only the RING between the circles is shaded.

The signs are \(\ge\) and \(\le\) (not \(>\) or \(<\)), so the boundary circles belong to the region: draw them SOLID. This is the diagram below, with radii 1 and 2 marked on the \(\mathrm{Re}\) axis.

questions.hint: \(\arg z=\theta\) is a RAY from the origin at angle \(\theta\) from the positive \(\mathrm{Re}\) axis (measured anticlockwise). The inequality gives all rays with angle BETWEEN \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (\(45^{\circ}\)) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) (\(135^{\circ}\)): a wedge. Strict \(>\) and \(<\) mean the edges are DASHED.

steps.explain: \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}=45^{\circ}\) is the ray at \(45^{\circ}\) (through \((1,1)\)); \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=135^{\circ}\) is the ray through \((-1,1)\).
steps.work: \(\arg z=\dfrac{\pi}{4}:\ y=x,\ x>0;\qquad\arg z=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}:\ y=-x,\ x<0\)

steps.explain: Rewrite as \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}<\arg z<\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\): the angle must be larger than \(45^{\circ}\) and smaller than \(135^{\circ}\), so the region is the wedge ABOVE the origin between the two rays (it contains the positive imaginary axis, \(\arg=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)).
Both inequalities are STRICT, so the two rays are NOT included: draw them dashed. The origin itself has no argument, so it is also excluded.
This gives the dashed wedge shown below, opening upward.

steps.explain: Why not the others: A has solid rays (that would be \(\le\)); B is the wedge below the axis (\(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}<\arg z<-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)); D is the large wedge going the long way round (\(\arg z>\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) or \(<\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Rays at \(45^{\circ}\) and \(135^{\circ}\); strict inequality = dashed.

questions.stem: On separate Argand diagrams sketch the following loci: \(3\ge\mathrm{Re}\,z\ge0\) and \(3\ge\mathrm{Im}\,z\ge1\). Which diagram shows this locus?

questions.hint: \(\mathrm{Re}\,z=x\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,z=y\). The first inequality limits \(x\) to a vertical strip, the second limits \(y\) to a horizontal strip. “And” means BOTH must hold — the overlap of the strips is a rectangle with solid edges.

steps.explain: Write \(z=x+iy\), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,z=x\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,z=y\).
\(0\le x\le3\): the vertical strip between the lines \(x=0\) (the \(\mathrm{Im}\) axis) and \(x=3\).
\(1\le y\le3\): the horizontal strip between the lines \(y=1\) and \(y=3\).
“And” means the points in BOTH strips: a rectangle with corners \((0,1),(3,1),(3,3),(0,3)\). All inequalities are \(\ge\)/\(\le\), so every edge is SOLID.

questions.stem: It is given that \(|z-1-i|=1\). What is the maximum value of \(\mathrm{Arg}\,(z)\)?
questions.hint: \(|z-(1+i)|=1\) is a circle: centre \(1+i\), radius \(1\). Sketch it and find the point of the circle that makes the LARGEST angle with the positive real axis at the origin.

steps.explain: \(|z-w|=r\) is the circle with centre \(w\) and radius \(r\). Here \(z-1-i=z-(1+i)\), so the centre is \((1,1)\) and the radius is 1.

questions.stem: Which of the following Argand diagrams describes the relationship defined by \(\arg(z-i)=\arg(z+1)\)?
questions.hint: \(\arg(z-i)\) is the direction of the arrow from \(i\) TO \(z\); \(\arg(z+1)\) is the direction of the arrow from \(-1\) TO \(z\). They are EQUAL when both arrows point the SAME way. Find the line through \(i\) and \(-1\), then decide which parts of it work (watch the open circles).

steps.explain: Both arrows start from points on the line through \(-1\) and \(i\): gradient \(\dfrac{1-0}{0-(-1)}=1\), so the line is \(y=x+1\).

If \(z\) is beyond \(i\) (upper right), both arrows (red from \(i\), orange from \(-1\)) point at \(45^{\circ}\): equal arguments ✓. If \(z\) is beyond \(-1\) (lower left) both point at \(-135^{\circ}\): equal ✓.
steps.work: \(z\text{ on the line outside the segment from }-1\text{ to }i\)

steps.explain: If \(z\) is BETWEEN \(-1\) and \(i\) the arrows point in OPPOSITE directions (arguments differ by \(\pi\)): not allowed. At \(z=i\) and \(z=-1\) one argument is undefined: OPEN circles at \((0,1)\) and \((-1,0)\).
Why not the others: B and D are on the line \(y=x-1\) (wrong line); C is the segment BETWEEN \(-1\) and \(i\) (opposite arrows).
So the correct choice is option A.

UNION means “either/or”: shade a point if it is in at least ONE of the regions.

steps.explain: Region 1: the wedge above the origin between the rays at \(30^{\circ}\) and \(150^{\circ}\) (boundaries included).
Region 2: centre \((0,1)\), radius 2: the circle passes through \((0,-1)\), \((0,3)\) and \((\pm\sqrt3,0)\); shade the EXTERIOR (boundary included).
UNION: shade everything in the wedge, PLUS everything outside the circle. The only UNshaded part is inside the circle but outside the wedge.

questions.stem: The equation, in Cartesian form, of the locus of the point \(z\) if \(|z+2i|=|z+4|\) is:
questions.hint: \(|z-w|\) is the distance from \(z\) to \(w\). Here \(z\) is equally far from \(-2i\) and \(-4\), so the locus is a perpendicular bisector. Or substitute \(z=x+iy\) and square both sides.

steps.explain: Write \(z=x+iy\) and group real and imaginary parts: \(z+2i=x+(y+2)i\) and \(z+4=(x+4)+yi\).
Square both sides (modulus squared = real\(^2\) + imaginary\(^2\)).
Expand each bracket.
Cancel \(x^{2}+y^{2}\) from both sides and collect terms on the left.

Geometric check: the locus is the perpendicular bisector of \(A(0,-2)\) and \(B(-4,0)\). The midpoint is \(M(-2,-1)\); gradient of \(AB=-\dfrac{1}{2}\), so the bisector has gradient 2: \(y+1=2(x+2)\), i.e. \(2x-y+3=0\) ✓.

questions.hint: \(|z-w|=r\) is a CIRCLE with centre \(w\) and radius \(r\). Read the centre from the bracket (careful with the signs) and the radius from the right-hand side. Then check whether the circle passes through the origin: the distance from the centre to \(O\) is \(\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}}\).

steps.explain: Read the equation as “the distance from \(z\) to \(4+3i\) is 5”: centre \(4+3i\), i.e. the point \((4,3)\), radius 5.
Special feature (the 3-4-5 triangle): the distance from the centre to the origin is \(\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}}=5=r\), so the circle PASSES THROUGH THE ORIGIN.

questions.hint: \(|z|\) is the distance from \(O\) to \(P\). On a circle through \(O\), the farthest point from \(O\) is the other end of the DIAMETER that starts at \(O\), so it lies on the line from \(O\) through the centre.

steps.explain: The circle has centre \(C(4,3)\) and passes through \(O\) (since \(|OC|=\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}}=5=r\)). So \(OC\) is a radius.
The farthest point \(P\) from \(O\) is where the line \(OC\) meets the circle again: the diameter from \(O\) has length \(2r=10\), so \(|z|_{\max}=10\) and \(P=2C=(8,6)\).
\(\arg z\) is the angle \(\theta\) of the ray \(OP\) from the positive real axis. Use \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}\) with the centre (or \(P\)): both give the same ratio.

questions.stem: A point \(P\), which moves in the complex plane, is represented by the equation \(|z-(4+3i)|=5\). Find the modulus of \(z\) when \(\arg z=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\).
questions.hint: \(\arg z=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}\) only tells you the DIRECTION of \(z\): it lies on the ray \(y=\dfrac{x}{3}\), \(x>0\). The point must ALSO be on the circle, so find where the ray meets the circle (not just \(3+i\)).

steps.explain: The ray at angle \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}\) has \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(y=\dfrac{x}{3}\).
Substitute into the circle \((x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=25\).
\(x=0\) is the origin (not a valid argument); the other solution is \(x=9\), so \(y=\dfrac{9}{3}=3\).

questions.stem: A subset of the complex plane is described by the relation \(\operatorname{Arg}(z-2i)=\dfrac\pi6\). Find the Cartesian equation of this relation.
questions.hint: Put \(z=x+iy\), so \(z-2i=x+(y-2)i\). Its argument is \(\dfrac\pi6\), so \(\tan\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\text{imaginary}}{\text{real}}\). The argument \(\dfrac\pi6\) is in the 1st quadrant, so the real part \(x\) must be POSITIVE.

steps.explain: Write \(z=x+iy\) and combine the imaginary parts.
\(\operatorname{Arg}=\dfrac\pi6\) means \(\tan\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{y-2}{x}\) with \(x>0\) (1st quadrant: real and imaginary parts both positive).
Solve for \(y\).
Restriction: since the argument is \(\dfrac\pi6\) (not \(\dfrac\pi6-\pi\)), the point must be to the right of \(2i\): \(x>0\). So we have a RAY, not a full line.

Why not the others: B uses \(\tan\dfrac\pi6=\sqrt3\) (it is \(\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\)); C has \(-2\) (the point is \(z-2i\), so the start is \(+2i\)); D is the full line, which would also include \(\operatorname{Arg}=\dfrac\pi6-\pi\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the Cartesian equation of this relation
keyPoints.note: \(\tan\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{y-2}{x}\); \(x>0\).

questions.stem: A subset of the complex plane is described by the relation \(\operatorname{Arg}(z-2i)=\dfrac\pi6\). Which diagram is a sketch of this relation?
questions.hint: \(\operatorname{Arg}(z-w)=\theta\) is a RAY that starts at \(w\) (the point \(w\) itself is NOT included, so draw an open circle there) and makes the angle \(\theta\) with the positive real direction. Here the start is \(w=2i\) and \(\theta=\dfrac\pi6=30^{\circ}\).

steps.explain: Starting point: \(z-2i=0\) when \(z=2i\), i.e. \((0,2)\). The argument of \(0\) is undefined, so this point is EXCLUDED: open circle.
Direction: from \((0,2)\), a ray at \(30^{\circ}\) above the horizontal (gradient \(\tan30^{\circ}=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\approx0.58\), gently rising) going to the RIGHT (\(x>0\)).

Why not the others: B has gradient \(\sqrt3\) (a \(60^{\circ}\) ray); C starts at the origin (that would be \(\operatorname{Arg}z=\dfrac\pi6\)); D is a full line, but the argument condition gives only the ray on the right of \(2i\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Which diagram is a sketch of this relation
keyPoints.note: Ray from \(2i\) at \(30^{\circ}\); open circle at the start.

questions.hint: \(\arg\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=\arg(z-1)-\arg(z+1)\) is the ANGLE at \(z\) between the lines to \(-1\) and \(1\) (the chord). A constant angle subtended by a chord means an ARC of a circle through \(1\) and \(-1\) (inscribed-angle theorem).

steps.explain: \(\arg(z-1)-\arg(z+1)=\dfrac\pi4>0\): the angle at \(z\) subtended by the interval from \(-1\) to \(1\) is \(\dfrac\pi4\), and it is measured the positive way, so \(z\) is ABOVE the real axis (\(y>0\)).

Inscribed angle theorem: the CENTRAL angle on the same chord is double, \(\dfrac\pi2\). The chord has length 2, so \(2=2r\sin\dfrac\pi4\), giving \(r=\sqrt2\). The centre lies on the perpendicular bisector (the \(y\)-axis) at distance \(\sqrt{r^{2}-1}=1\) from the chord.

Since the angle \(\dfrac\pi4\) is SMALLER than \(\dfrac\pi2\), the points are on the MAJOR arc (the longer arc, which contains the part of the circle above the centre). The points \(\pm1\) are excluded (\(\arg\) is undefined there): open circles.

steps.explain: Check: \(z=i\left(1+\sqrt2\right)\) (the top of the circle): \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=\dfrac{-1+ti}{1+ti}\) with \(t=1+\sqrt2\), whose argument is \(\dfrac\pi4\) ✓.

Why not the others: B is the MINOR arc above the axis (centre \((0,-1)\)); there the angle is \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). C is the whole circle (the lower arc gives \(\arg=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\)). D is the lower major arc, where the argument is NEGATIVE.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Constant angle on chord \([-1,1]\): major arc, centre \((0,1)\), \(r=\sqrt2\).

questions.hint: Larger angle subtended by the chord means CLOSER to the chord. \(\arg=\dfrac\pi2\) (a right angle) happens on the circle with diameter \([-1,1]\) (the UNIT circle, by Thales). So \(\dfrac\pi4\le\arg\le\dfrac\pi2\) lies BETWEEN the unit semicircle and the \(\dfrac\pi4\) arc.

steps.explain: Boundary \(\arg=\dfrac\pi2\): the angle at \(z\) is a right angle, so \(z\) lies on the circle with DIAMETER from \(-1\) to \(1\) (Thales): the upper unit semicircle \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\), \(y>0\).
Boundary \(\arg=\dfrac\pi4\): the major arc from part (i).

Inside the unit circle the angle is BIGGER than \(\dfrac\pi2\) (points close to the chord); outside the big circle it is SMALLER than \(\dfrac\pi4\). So we need the points OUTSIDE the unit semicircle but INSIDE the big arc.

Test point \(z=1.2i\): outside the unit circle, inside the big circle. \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=\dfrac{-1+1.2i}{1+1.2i}\) has argument \(129.8^{\circ}-50.2^{\circ}\approx79.6^{\circ}\), which is between \(45^{\circ}\) and \(90^{\circ}\) ✓.

steps.explain: Why not the others: B shades the inside of the unit semicircle (\(\arg>\dfrac\pi2\)); C shades the outside of the big circle (\(\arg<\dfrac\pi4\)); D shades everything inside the big circle, including the part with \(\arg>\dfrac\pi2\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Between the unit semicircle and the \(\dfrac\pi4\) arc (above the axis).
